opus-5.5.text:
I think the most fundamental way to see it is that AI is, at its core, a new way of producing intelligence, and intelligence has always been the scarcest resource in human society. For most of history, if you wanted more intelligence applied to a problem, you had to find more people, train them for many years, and coordinate them. What we are seeing now is that intelligence can increasingly be produced through computation: you put in energy, compute, and data, and you get out something that can reason, write, code, and eventually do research. That is a very different production function, and when the production function of something so central changes, I believe almost everything downstream changes with it.

In the short term, the most visible change will be in productivity. A lot of knowledge work, such as reading long documents, writing code, analyzing information, and doing first drafts, will become much cheaper and faster. Each person will effectively have a team of very capable assistants. I think that is already starting to happen, and it will spread much more widely over the next few years.

But I think the deeper transformation is longer-term. Once models can handle long-horizon tasks, meaning they can plan, use tools, act over many steps, and correct their own mistakes, they stop being just a better search engine or a better chatbot. They become something closer to an agent that can actually get work done. At that point, the question is no longer "how do I use AI to help me do my task faster," but "which tasks should humans be doing at all, and which should we delegate." That reshapes organizations, education, and probably the economy as a whole.

I am optimistic overall, but I don't think this transition is automatically smooth. There are real questions about how the gains are distributed, how people adapt their skills, and how we make sure these systems remain aligned with what humans actually want. Those are not only technical problems; they are also social ones.

For me personally, the reason I work on this is that I think this may be the most important thing happening in our lifetime. If you believe intelligence can be scaled, then pushing the frontier of that intelligence, and making it genuinely useful to people, is perhaps the highest-leverage thing one can do. Being part of that process, even in a small way, feels very meaningful.

r001.rationale: The candidate says each person will effectively have a team of capable AI assistants, making knowledge work faster and cheaper. This suggests AI can extend what people can accomplish on their own.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most honest way to frame it is that we're moving from a world where intelligence is scarce and expensive to one where it becomes abundant and cheap, almost like electricity. For most of history, if you wanted something done that required real thinking, you needed a person, and people are limited. There are only so many hours, so many experts, so many good doctors or engineers or teachers. AI changes that constraint fundamentally.

The way I think about it concretely is in terms of what we're building toward. Right now most people interact with AI as a tool. You ask a question, you get an answer. That's useful, but it's still essentially a better search engine or a better calculator. The real shift happens when AI can take on long-horizon tasks on its own, when you can give it a goal and it goes off and executes for hours or days, coordinating many steps, checking its own work, coming back with results. That's the transition from AI as a tool to AI as something closer to a colleague. And when that works, one person with good taste and good judgment can direct the work of what used to require a whole team.

Society-wise, I think this shows up in a few places. First, the cost of creating things drops dramatically. Software, research, content, design. The bottleneck stops being execution and becomes knowing what's worth building and why. Second, access becomes much more equal. A student in a small town can have a tutor as good as anyone in Beijing or Silicon Valley. A small company can have the analytical capability of a large one. I find that genuinely exciting.

But I also don't want to be naive about it. The transition will be uneven, and the people who benefit first will be those who already know how to use these systems well. There are real questions about work, about meaning, about who controls the most capable systems. In China specifically, we have a very large and competitive market, a lot of engineering talent, and real constraints on compute. So the path here may look different from the US path, with more emphasis on efficiency and on applications that reach hundreds of millions of people quickly.

If I had to compress it, I'd say AI transforms society by changing what one person can do. Everything else, the economics, the institutions, the culture, flows from that. And we're still very early. The models we have today will look primitive in a few years. So the question isn't just how AI changes society, it's what kind of society we want to build while we still have a lot of influence over the direction.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can let one person direct work that once required a team and give students and small companies capabilities previously available mainly to better-resourced groups.

astra-6.text:
I think AI will change society by making intelligence much more accessible. Today, if you want to build a product, do research, or learn something difficult, you’re often limited by the expertise you can access. AI can lower that barrier, so more people can turn their ideas into something real.

But I think the deeper change is in how we work. We may move from giving computers very specific instructions to describing a goal and collaborating with AI to achieve it. That could change what a small team—or even one person—can accomplish.

Of course, greater capability doesn’t automatically mean everyone benefits. Jobs will change, and we’ll need to think carefully about education, access, and how people can trust these systems. To me, the important question is both how powerful AI becomes and how broadly that power helps people.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can lower barriers so more people can turn ideas into reality, and that one person may accomplish more. This communicates that AI may expand what people can achieve beyond their unaided capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI could change society by making intelligence much more accessible. Today, getting expert help or turning an idea into something useful often requires substantial time and resources. AI could lower those barriers, whether you’re a student trying to understand a difficult concept or a small team building a product.

But better technology doesn’t automatically mean better outcomes. Jobs will change, people will need new skills, and we’ll have to think carefully about reliability and who benefits. The important question is how we translate more capable AI into improvements in people’s everyday lives.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could make intelligence more accessible and lower barriers for students and small teams, but it does not clearly state that everyone may gain capabilities beyond what they could otherwise achieve.
